strengths: Clear and useful idea: truncated polynomial classifiers provide a natural extension of linear probes that can be evaluated progressively, enabling both fixed safety-budget operation and input-adaptive cascades.

The method is technically simple, well motivated, and relatively easy to implement; the symmetric CP parameterization makes higher-order polynomial terms tractable and connects cleanly to attribution over activation dimensions.

The experimental coverage is reasonably strong: two safety datasets, four base LLMs, multiple layers, five seeds for the main comparisons, and baselines including linear probes, bilinear probes, parameter-matched MLP probes, and early-exit MLPs.

The progressive-training ablation is convincing and directly supports a central methodological claim: naive full-polynomial training does not yield reliable truncations, while the proposed degree-wise scheme does.
The paper includes useful additional analyses, including rank, maximum-degree, symmetric-vs-nonsymmetric CP, calibration, latency/throughput, and per-harm-category breakdowns.
The writing is generally clear, and the framing of safety monitoring as a dynamic compute allocation problem is timely and relevant.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than major. Polynomial probes, low-rank polynomial networks, early exits, and cascaded classifiers are established; the main contribution is their combination for activation-based safety monitoring with progressive training.

The central efficiency claim is only partially established. Many plots use parameter count as a proxy for compute, and although latency/throughput is later benchmarked, the adaptive cascade evaluation is still mostly framed in parameter-count terms rather than end-to-end serving cost, memory movement, batching behavior, or integration with real LLM inference.

The evaluation is limited to offline harmful/harmless prompt classification from existing datasets. It does not test robustness under adaptive jailbreaks, distribution shift, multilingual prompts, prompt obfuscation, model outputs, or online deployment settings where safety monitors are most consequential.

The comparison set omits important practical baselines such as lightweight text classifiers, distilled safety classifiers, LLM-as-judge monitors at realistic budgets, or hybrid text-plus-activation monitors. This makes it hard to judge deployment competitiveness beyond activation-probe baselines.

The interpretability claims are somewhat overstated. Attribution to dense residual-stream neuron coordinates or pairs is faithful to the classifier algebra, but the paper does not show that these attributions are semantically meaningful, stable, actionable, or useful for debugging safety failures.

The method assumes white-box access to internal activations and uses mean-pooled residual stream representations, but the paper does not deeply examine sensitivity to pooling choice, token position, prompt length, generation-time monitoring, or models where such access is unavailable.

The reported gains are sometimes modest on aggregate, especially relative to strong baselines, and some of the most striking improvements are per-category results that may involve small sample sizes; confidence intervals or significance tests would strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete as presented: the abstract says code is available but the link appears blank, and some implementation details needed to fully reproduce activation extraction and preprocessing are only lightly specified.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant problem: activation-based safety monitors have a useful cost/performance trade-off, and dynamic evaluation is a natural direction for always-on monitoring.
The proposed truncated polynomial classifier is technically coherent and easy to understand, with a straightforward progressive training scheme that makes intermediate truncations usable.

The empirical section covers multiple base models, two safety datasets, two layers per model in the appendix, rank/order ablations, and comparisons to linear probes, bilinear probes, MLP probes, and early-exit MLPs.
The paper is generally clearly written, and the appendix provides useful implementation and computational-cost details.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core ingredients are low-rank polynomial networks, polynomial probes, progressive/layer-wise training, and early-exit cascades; the paper mainly combines these known ideas for activation monitoring, without a deeper technical advance.

The main evidence does not justify the strong safety framing. Evaluation is limited to supervised harmful-prompt classification on static datasets; there is no robustness testing against adaptive jailbreaks, distribution shift, cross-dataset transfer, adversarial prompt variants, or real deployment settings where safety monitors are most relevant.

The compute claims are weakly supported. Much of the paper uses parameter count as a proxy for inference cost, which is especially questionable when comparing polynomial terms, MLPs, activation extraction, batching, and hardware behavior. The latency appendix partially addresses this, but the headline cascade claims still rest heavily on an imperfect proxy.

The baselines are incomplete for a safety-monitoring paper. The work does not compare against strong external moderation models, LLM-as-judge monitors, prompt/text classifiers, SAE-feature probes, calibrated ensembles, or modern lightweight safety classifiers, so it is unclear whether TPCs are competitive beyond a narrow probe family.

Reported gains appear modest and sometimes hard to assess from plots alone. The paper emphasizes up to 10% subcategory improvements, but many aggregate improvements over linear/MLP baselines are small, no confidence intervals or significance tests are provided, and subcategory results may have small sample sizes.

The interpretability claim is overstated. Attributing logits to dense neuron-pair interactions is mechanically faithful to the classifier, but the examples are not semantically interpreted or validated, and the authors themselves note that the resulting neuron combinations lack human legibility.

The method depends on labeled safety data and chosen internal layers for each target model, but the paper does not sufficiently study data efficiency, layer-selection sensitivity, transfer across models/layers, or maintenance under model updates.
Reproducibility is weakened by the apparent missing/blank code URL in the abstract and by presenting many results as figures without tables of exact values.

strengths: Clear and timely problem framing: the paper targets a real limitation of activation-space safety monitors, namely fixed compute regardless of input difficulty or safety budget.
The proposed truncated polynomial classifier is technically simple, well motivated, and naturally generalizes linear probes while supporting both fixed-budget truncation and adaptive cascading.

Experimental coverage is reasonably broad for an activation-monitoring paper: two large safety datasets, four LLMs up to 30B parameters, multiple layers, multiple seeds, and comparisons to linear, bilinear, MLP, and early-exit MLP probes.

The progressive training ablation is convincing and supports an important part of the method: jointly trained polynomials do not reliably yield useful truncations, while the proposed degree-wise training does.

The paper includes useful implementation and analysis details, including parameter/FLOP derivations, latency/throughput checks, rank/order ablations, calibration plots, and symmetric vs non-symmetric CP comparisons.
The feature-attribution angle is appealing: polynomial terms provide faithful classifier-level attributions to neuron interactions, which is more transparent than generic MLP probes.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high. The work combines known ingredients, polynomial probes/networks, low-rank tensor factorization, progressive/greedy training, and early-exit cascading, with the main novelty being their packaging for LLM safety monitoring.

The evaluation is mostly limited to offline harmful-prompt classification on two public datasets. It does not test realistic deployment settings such as jailbreak transfer, distribution shift, adversarial adaptation against the monitor, multilingual prompts, or output-side monitoring.

The paper does not compare against important practical safety-monitoring baselines such as text classifiers, LlamaGuard/WildGuard-style LLM moderators, smaller distilled guard models, or hybrid systems. This weakens claims about safety monitoring broadly, even if activation-probe comparisons are strong.

The compute story is somewhat incomplete. Parameter count is an imperfect proxy for monitoring cost, and the activation extraction cost of running the target LLM dominates in many settings. The claimed flexibility is most compelling only when internal activations are already available or prompt-prefill cost is acceptable.

The safety claims are stronger than the evidence. Higher F1 on benchmark labels does not establish stronger guardrails under adaptive misuse, nor does it address false-negative costs, threshold selection under deployment constraints, or robustness to prompt distribution changes.

Interpretability claims should be tempered. The attributions are faithful to the probe computation, but the identified dense neuron interactions are not semantically interpretable without further analysis, so the practical transparency benefit remains limited.

Some results appear to show relatively modest absolute gains over strong baselines, especially on BeaverTails, and the paper would benefit from clearer statistical reporting and tabular summaries rather than relying heavily on dense plots.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: making activation-based safety monitors more flexible under different inference-time budgets.

The proposed TPC formulation is simple, coherent, and practically attractive: it exactly recovers linear probes at first order while allowing progressively richer polynomial interactions and early exits.

The experimental section is fairly broad, covering 4 base LLMs, 2 large safety datasets, multiple layers, 5 seeds, MLP/early-exit MLP/bilinear baselines, and several appendices with cross-dataset, latency, rank, degree, and training ablations.
The progressive training ablation is convincing: standard end-to-end polynomial training does not produce useful truncations, while the proposed stage-wise training does.
The cascade evaluation is a useful practical contribution, showing that many examples can exit early with performance close to the full polynomial.
The paper is clearly written overall, with enough mathematical and implementation detail to understand and likely reproduce the method, assuming code is released.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than strong. Polynomial probes, low-rank CP parameterizations, symmetric tensor factorizations, and early-exit cascades are all established; the main contribution is their combination for dynamic safety monitoring.

The empirical gains over strong baselines are often small. On the main static results, TPCs improve over MLP/EE-MLP by fractions of an F1 point on WildGuardMix and are sometimes slightly worse on BeaverTails. This weakens claims of clear superiority.

The paper overstates interpretability. The attribution example identifies dense interactions among raw neuron indices, but these are not semantically interpreted or validated. Being faithful to the probe computation is not the same as providing human-meaningful safety explanations.

Compute is mostly measured by monitor parameter count, which is an imperfect proxy for latency, memory movement, and real deployment cost. The appendix latency results help, but the main claims around compute-efficient safety would be stronger with fuller wall-clock and end-to-end serving measurements.

The safety evaluation is limited to binary prompt classification datasets. There is little evidence for robustness under adaptive attacks, jailbreak distributions, output-side monitoring, multi-turn contexts, or deployment settings where adversaries may optimize against the monitor.

The paper relies heavily on F1 as the primary metric. For safety monitoring, false negatives, false positives, calibration under distribution shift, threshold selection, and operating-point tradeoffs should be central rather than mostly secondary.

The cascade thresholding strategy appears simple and useful, but the procedure for choosing thresholds and its sensitivity across datasets/deployments is not explored deeply enough for the strength of the safety-dial framing.
Reproducibility is mostly good in terms of described hyperparameters, but the manuscript text shows the code URL as blank, so actual artifact availability is unclear from the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: making activation-space safety monitors more flexible than a fixed linear probe, with a clear framing around fixed-budget and input-adaptive monitoring.
The proposed TPC formulation is simple and fairly well explained. The progressive evaluation/training idea gives a coherent way to obtain nested classifiers from one polynomial model.

The experiments cover multiple base models, two large safety datasets, several layers, multiple random seeds for the main static comparisons, and include ablations for progressive training, rank, degree, calibration, latency, and cross-dataset evaluation.
The paper compares against reasonable local baselines, including linear probes, bilinear probes, parameter-matched MLP probes, and early-exit MLPs.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method is essentially a low-rank polynomial probe with early-exit/truncated evaluation and progressive training, combining well-known ingredients rather than introducing a substantially new monitoring paradigm.

The empirical gains are modest and sometimes marginal. In the main static table, TPC improves over the strongest MLP/EE-MLP baselines by only small fractions on several settings, and on BeaverTails it is not consistently best on test F1.

The compute story is not fully convincing. Parameter count is used as the primary proxy for compute, while practical monitoring cost depends on activation extraction, memory movement, batching, layer access, latency, and deployment constraints. The paper partially benchmarks latency, but the main claims still lean heavily on an abstract proxy.

The evaluation is mostly offline binary prompt classification on curated datasets. For a safety-monitoring paper, there is little evidence under realistic deployment conditions, adaptive adversaries, jailbreak distributions, response-level monitoring, threshold policies, or end-to-end impact on harmful completions and benign refusal rates.

The interpretability claims are overstated. The attribution is faithful to the probe’s polynomial terms, but the neuron-pair examples are not human-legible and do not establish mechanistic understanding of the underlying LLM features.

The comparison to LLM-as-monitor baselines is weak and framed too favorably: the external LLMs are not fine-tuned, prompts are only lightly optimized, parameter counts are guessed from public speculation, and the comparison is relegated to preliminary appendix results.

Reproducibility is concerning: the manuscript says code is available, but the extracted PDF shows a blank link. Important implementation choices for activation extraction, preprocessing, thresholds, and exact splits would need to be available for a top-tier submission.

The safety framing is stronger than the evidence. The paper claims stronger guardrails and dynamic safety monitoring, but the experiments primarily show small F1 improvements on labels, not robust safety improvements in deployed LLM behavior.

The method introduces additional hyperparameters and selection burden, including layer choice, polynomial degree, CP rank, thresholds, and progressive training schedule. The paper acknowledges layer search but does not sufficiently address how this affects practical use.

The ethics section is too thin for a paper about safety classifiers. It does not seriously discuss failure modes, false refusals, distribution shift, misuse of safety labels, adaptive evasion, or overreliance on internal monitors.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful extension of linear activation probes: truncated polynomial classifiers that can be evaluated progressively, giving both fixed budget and input adaptive monitoring modes from a single trained model.

The experimental section is substantially stronger than average: results cover two safety datasets, four base LLMs up to 30B parameters, multiple layers, parameter matched MLP and early exit MLP baselines, cascade evaluation, cross dataset transfer, calibration, latency/throughput, rank/order ablations, and progressive training ablations.
The method is simple, well motivated, and practically relevant for safety monitoring, where cheap always on guards and stronger conditional checks are both desirable.
The progressive training ablation convincingly supports a central technical claim: standard polynomial training does not reliably yield good truncations, while the proposed degree wise training does.
The paper is generally well written and carefully positioned, with useful implementation details and a reasonable limitations section.
weaknesses: The core novelty is moderate rather than major: the work combines known ingredients, including polynomial probes, low rank CP parameterization, progressive/greedy training, and early exit cascades. The paper’s main contribution is a well executed application and packaging of these ideas for LLM safety monitoring rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The empirical gains over strong baselines are often modest. On WildGuardMix the improvements over MLP/EE-MLP are positive but small, and on BeaverTails TPCs are sometimes slightly behind EE-MLPs. This weakens the case for a clear Accept despite the breadth of evaluation.

The compute story is somewhat incomplete. Parameter count is used as the main proxy for test time cost, but in deployment the cost of extracting activations from the base LLM, memory movement, batching regime, and latency constraints matter. The appendix latency results help, but the main claims about compute efficient safety would be stronger with more deployment realistic accounting.

The interpretability claim is only partially convincing. The attribution is faithful to the polynomial probe, but the demonstrated neuron pair interactions are dense and not semantically interpretable; this is more transparency of the classifier computation than actionable mechanistic understanding.

The safety evaluation is limited to offline prompt classification benchmarks. The paper does not test adaptive adversaries, jailbreak distribution shifts beyond standard datasets, output monitoring, or thresholded operating points such as precision/recall/false rejection tradeoffs under realistic moderation requirements.

Reproducibility is weakened by an apparently missing or redacted code URL in the manuscript, despite the reproducibility statement claiming code availability. More details on exact splits, preprocessing, and saved activations would also help.

Some design choices remain under explored in the main paper, including mean pooling over tokens, layer selection, monotonicity failures when increasing order, and whether simpler polynomial feature expansions or kernelized/nonlinear probes could match the observed gains.
